S. S. Halder. A. Y. Mashiuzzaman ----- For the Petitioner.
K. A. Wahab, Deputy Advocate- General--For State.
parties:
Md. Khalilur Rahman  ----- Petitioner
Vs.
The State  ----- Opp. parties.
full_judgment: 6. The first contention of Mr. Halder, the learned Advocate is that the offence alleged against the accused petitioner relates to the period when the State of Bangladesh did not come into existence not to speak of the First Proclamation and as such it is beyond the scope of the Martial Law Regulations, it is necessary in this connection to look into the First Proclamation of 20th August, 1975. It is from the 15th August 1975 when the full powers of the Government was assumed by Khondkar Moshtaque Ahmed, the then President of the Republic of Bangladesh. It is again from the 15th of August. 1975 that the whole Bangladesh was places under the Martial Law by a declaration broadcast from all the stations of Radio 13angladesb and it is again from the morning of 15th August the then President Khondkar Mostaque Ahmed suspended certain articles of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh namely, part of Article 48 and whole of Article 55 and also modified article 148 and form 1 of the Third Schedule rewarding the oath of office of the President. The Second Proclamation of the 8th November 1975 by Mr. Justice Abusadat Mohammad Salem, the then President of Bangladesh, spoke of the 6th November 1975 as well as 15th August. 1975 from which date, by the Second Proclamation Martial Law so promulgated was kept in force. The Third Proclamation which came into force on 29th November. 1976 by Mr. Justice Abused Mohammad Sayem by which the office of the Chief Martial Law Administrator was handed over from the then President Major General Ziaur Rahman B.U. PSC speaks of the earlier two Proclamations of 20th August, 1975 and 8th November, 1975. The cardinal point that emerges from these three proclamations is that the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh excepting in certain parts was kept intact for the purpose of administration of this country along with some Martial Law Regulations. The submission of the learned Deputy Advocate General is that because of the use of the word "before" occurring in Martiai Law Regulation No.11 the offences committed at any historical time, if only legal evidence can be brought before court are tribal under the Martial Law Regulations, is, in our opinion, difficult to accept because for this proposition the learned Deputy Advocate General has neither relied upon any well-settled principles of jurisprudence nor any decision of any superior court. As a matter of fact the learned Deputy Advocate-General made submissions only. The allegations taken at its earliest against the accused petitioner do not go beyond the period of 1952 when he assumed the office of Tehsildar of Puthia Raj Estate in 1952 and the latest is in 1952. The country as it then was in 1952 was the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. For the purpose of administration of the country there had been successive Constitutions and Martial Law to govern the country. The State of People's Republic of Bangladesh was established after proclaiming independence en the 26th March 1971. The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was adopted enacted by the Constituent Assembly on the 4th November, 1972. The Constitution having been kept intact by the three successive proclamations except in certain minor parts we cannot see how offences committed by a person in a different State, under a different Government could be brought within the scope of Martial Law Regulations proclaimed on the 15th August, 1975. The argument of the learned Deputy Advocate General has a builtin absurdity inasmuch as according to him if it is possible to bring legal evidence of offences committed even in British India those offences can also be tried under the present Martial Law Regulations. In interpreting a penal statute which is made effective retrospectively reference may be made to paragraph 645 at page 425 of Halsbury's Laws of England volume 38, Third Edition which runs thus : "The presumption against retrospection applies in general to legislation of a penal character, and to be presumed that a statute creating a new offence or extending an existing one, is not intended to render seminal an act which was innocent when it was committed and that a statute increasing the penalties for existing offences is not intended to apply to offences committed before its commencement."
